briefing.question: Who should decide when a nation goes to war and when it stops, and what makes a war just to continue?
briefing.agreed: Troops may be defended, but a sustained war needs authority and an aim at peace.
briefing.split: Aquinas, cause and intent; Augustine, retaliation breeds evils; Hamilton, Congress decides; Grotius, does it bring peace nearer.

briefing.question: Can a free people be governed well by those who will not fight hard, or does hard fighting corrupt the people who wage it?
briefing.agreed: Politics needs strength, but how a party fights shapes whether it can govern after.
briefing.split: Machiavelli, know how to do wrong; Aristotle, civic friendship; Cicero, neither force nor fraud; Lincoln, malice toward none.

briefing.question: Is peace among the powerful worth a price paid by the weak?
briefing.agreed: Talks can lower risk, but peace cannot be bought by trading smaller nations.
briefing.split: Thucydides, the strong and the weak; Kissinger, balance and legitimacy; Kant, no state traded; Wilson, open covenants; Churchill, strength.

briefing.question: Does a society owe reverence to what its people hold sacred, or does freedom require that nothing be beyond depiction?
briefing.agreed: No legal suppression; believers may object, and a petition is speech too.
briefing.split: Mill, defend both, brand no one; Plato, stories form the young; Milton, freedom with limits; Tolstoy, judge by sincerity.

briefing.question: Are some subjects too grave for certain kinds of art, and who has the authority to decide?
briefing.agreed: Grave subjects are open to art, its handling open to judgment; no threats.
briefing.split: Aristotle, terrible not monstrous; Douglass, irony that keeps the enslaved human; Adorno, no comfort; Holmes, let critics decide.

briefing.question: Who has the first claim to shape a child's mind: the family, the state's schools or the child's own developing reason?
briefing.agreed: Elections can be taught, but a teacher should not celebrate one side.
briefing.split: Dewey, engage without partisanship; Weber, no preaching; Mill, beware state moulding; Leo XIII, parents first.

briefing.question: Is human finitude a flaw to be engineered away, or part of what makes us human?
briefing.agreed: Healing and longer life are good if shared; escaping limits raises hard questions.
briefing.split: Bacon, relief for all; Lewis, power over others; Aquinas, preserve not escape; Seneca, life is long if used well.

briefing.question: Should faith be kept private in shared public spaces, or does true freedom of religion include the freedom to profess it openly?
briefing.agreed: A club may set rules, but one standard for faith and every other message.
briefing.split: Locke, test the rule; Williams, guard faith from commerce; Rousseau, tolerate the tolerant; Rawls, no duty to hide faith.

briefing.question: What does justice owe the murdered, and may the state answer killing with killing?
briefing.agreed: A grave crime demands justice and fair process; the condemned keep dignity.
briefing.split: Kant, murder requires death; Beccaria, no right to kill; Aquinas, only if necessary; Augustine, plead mercy.

setup.text: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it launched six drones Sunday at a U.S. air-defense radar at a helicopter base in Bahrain, its second strike there in three days in retaliation for U.S. strikes; Bahrain said the drones were intercepted. sittings.why_these_chairs: Aquinas speaks first because the report names the just war conditions of Summa Theologiae II-II, Q. 40: authority, cause and right intention. Augustine follows because the report names him as the source of that tradition, and his City of God and Reply to Faustus say what a just war must aim at and what corrupts it. Hamilton is seated because the report names the constitutional split between Congress declaring war and the president commanding, and his Federalist No. 69 drew that line for the ratifiers. Grotius closes because the report names proportionality and the danger of tit-for-tat escalation, and his Rights of War and Peace limits force to what a war's lawful aim requires. Vegetius, whose maxim on preparing for war the report names, is noted but not seated; his text was not fetched here. Madison's war-powers letters were also not fetched, so Hamilton carries the constitutional point. The Revolutionary Guard, the governments and the congressman are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: who should decide when a nation goes to war and when it stops, and what makes a war just to continue? The other side is those who want the war ended, who say nine months of fighting without a clear goal or congressional authorization is exactly what the Constitution's war powers were meant to prevent, point to polls showing most Americans want Congress to end the conflict, and argue that each tit-for-tat strike risks a wider war with no exit. sittings.headline: Pope Leo XIV in Peru: transhumanism is a mirage for millionaires seeking immortality, and God made us male and female
sittings.question: Is human finitude a flaw to be engineered away, or part of what makes us human?

setup.text: On a trip to his adopted homeland, Pope Leo XIV told a Catholic university in Chiclayo on Nov. 13 that science must not become a privilege reserved for millionaires seeking immortality while entire peoples suffer, calling human limitation not a manufacturing defect but the very condition of human grandeur. Days earlier in Lima he said the Church must assert with greater conviction that God created the human person male and female, while condemning machismo, violence against women and the subordination of one spouse to the other. Both messages drew praise and pushback online this weekend.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Francis Bacon speaks first because the report names his project for the relief of man's estate, the founding statement of the hope that knowledge can lengthen life and conquer nature, from which the transhumanist hope descends. C. S. Lewis follows because the report names The Abolition of Man and its warning that man's conquest of nature becomes the power of some men over others; he is in copyright and is paraphrased. Aquinas is seated because the report names the natural-law tradition of human nature as given. Seneca closes because the report names On the Shortness of Life and the Stoic acceptance of mortality. Genesis 1:27 and Psalm 90, the first named by the report, are read by the moderator. Nick Bostrom, named for the transhumanist hope, is a living author and is left off; Bacon carries the case for extending life. The Pope and his critics are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: is human finitude a flaw to be engineered away, or part of what makes us human? The report gives one side as admirers, who say the Pope is defending a classic Christian anthropology against two temptations, denying the givenness of the body and the sexes and dreaming of escaping death through technology, and that accepting limits makes people humble, grateful and attentive to the weak, while his defense of women shows that tradition and dignity go together. Begin.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what does justice owe the murdered, and may the state answer killing with killing?
